scenes.tts: The cerebral cortex needs two kinds of neuron. Some excite their neighbours. Others inhibit them.
scenes.visual: Title card: Born Outside. A strip of cortex with green excitatory triangles and magenta inhibitory dots.
scenes.narration: The cerebral cortex needs two kinds of neuron. Some excite their neighbours. Others inhibit them.

scenes.tts: In rodents, roughly a fifth of cortical neurons are inhibitory interneurons.
scenes.visual: Counter on screen: about 1 in 5 cortical neurons is inhibitory. One dot in five lights up.
scenes.narration: In rodents, roughly a fifth of cortical neurons are inhibitory interneurons.

scenes.tts: Yet the cortex's own wall makes the excitatory kind. These pyramidal neurons climb straight out along radial glial fibres, long struts that span the wall.
scenes.visual: Cross-section of the cortical wall. Green triangles climb radial fibres from the ventricle to the surface.
scenes.narration: Yet the cortex's own wall makes the excitatory kind. These pyramidal neurons climb straight out along radial glial fibres, long struts that span the wall.

scenes.tts: So where do the inhibitory neurons come from?
scenes.visual: Question on screen: where do the inhibitory neurons come from? The magenta dots fade to outlines.
scenes.narration: So where do the inhibitory neurons come from?

scenes.tts: Start with a map. The dorsal part of the embryonic forebrain, the pallium, forms the cortex.
scenes.visual: Coronal section of an embryonic mouse forebrain at a rostral level, with a small rostrocaudal axis marker. The pallium is shaded green and labelled.
scenes.narration: Start with a map. The dorsal part of the embryonic forebrain, the pallium, forms the cortex.

scenes.tts: Its ventral part, the subpallium, bulges into the ventricle as three swellings.
scenes.visual: The subpallium is shaded magenta. In this rostral section two swellings bulge into the ventricle. The section plane then slides caudally, and a third swelling appears.
scenes.narration: Its ventral part, the subpallium, bulges into the ventricle as three swellings.

scenes.tts: These are the lateral, medial and caudal ganglionic eminences. Despite the name, they are not ganglia.
scenes.visual: Labels appear across the two levels: lateral and medial ganglionic eminences (LGE, MGE) in the rostral section, caudal ganglionic eminence (CGE) in the caudal one.
scenes.narration: These are the lateral, medial and caudal ganglionic eminences. Despite the name, they are not ganglia.

scenes.tts: They are temporary germinal zones, packed with dividing progenitors.
scenes.visual: The eminences fill with dividing cells, shown as dots splitting in two.
scenes.narration: They are temporary germinal zones, packed with dividing progenitors.

scenes.tts: Pallial progenitors make neurons that release glutamate. Subpallial progenitors make neurons that release gabba, the main inhibitory transmitter.
scenes.caption: Pallial progenitors make neurons that release glutamate. Subpallial progenitors make neurons that release GABA, the main inhibitory transmitter.
scenes.visual: Two labels: pallium makes glutamate neurons; subpallium makes GABA neurons.
scenes.narration: Pallial progenitors make neurons that release glutamate. Subpallial progenitors make neurons that release GABA, the main inhibitory transmitter.

scenes.tts: In rodents, most cortical interneurons are born in the medial and caudal eminences. Then they travel sideways into the cortex.
scenes.visual: A magenta dot leaves the medial eminence and travels sideways along a dotted path, around the striatum, into the cortex.
scenes.narration: In rodents, most cortical interneurons are born in the medial and caudal eminences. Then they travel sideways into the cortex.

scenes.tts: Moving parallel to the brain surface is called tangential migration.
scenes.visual: Label: tangential migration, parallel to the surface. Beside it, a faint green triangle climbing radially for contrast.
scenes.narration: Moving parallel to the brain surface is called tangential migration.

scenes.tts: Here is the idea to carry through this lesson.
scenes.visual: A card slides in: The one idea.
scenes.narration: Here is the idea to carry through this lesson.

scenes.tts: Born outside the cortex, steered by what the cell can read.
scenes.visual: Rule on screen, word by word: Born outside the cortex, steered by what the cell can read.
scenes.narration: Born outside the cortex, steered by what the cell can read.

scenes.tts: At the turns studied so far, the road holds a cue. The travelling cell carries what answers it.
scenes.visual: The dotted path shows two turns: round the striatum, and into a lane. At each, a cue symbol on the road meets a receptor on the travelling dot.
scenes.narration: At the turns studied so far, the road holds a cue. The travelling cell carries what answers it.

scenes.tts: So a fault can sit in the cell, which cannot answer. Or it can sit in the road, which lacks the cue.
scenes.visual: Split screen. Left: a dot with a broken receptor stalls on a normal road. Right: a normal dot stalls where the road's cue is missing.
scenes.narration: So a fault can sit in the cell, which cannot answer. Or it can sit in the road, which lacks the cue.

scenes.tts: Swapping tissue between normal and mutant animals tells you which.
scenes.visual: Both panels get a question mark and a tag: which one? Chapter two. No real-gene outcome is shown yet.
scenes.narration: Swapping tissue between normal and mutant animals tells you which.

scenes.tts: And in the cortex, the lane's chemokine signal helps keep a cell in the lane.
scenes.visual: Two glowing lanes in the cortex; dots stay inside while their receptors glow. Label: signalling is needed (not: signalling is all that is needed).
scenes.narration: And in the cortex, the lane's chemokine signal helps keep a cell in the lane.

scenes.tts: Hold on to that. The next chapters test it.
scenes.visual: The rule card shrinks to a corner badge.
scenes.narration: Hold on to that. The next chapters test it.

scenes.tts: One limit first. These results come from mice and rats.
scenes.visual: Badge: mouse and rat embryos.
scenes.narration: One limit first. These results come from mice and rats.

scenes.tts: In humans, the eminences are seen as the main source too. But cortical progenitors also make some inhibitory neurons.
scenes.visual: A human fetal forebrain outline: most magenta dots from the eminences, a few from the cortical wall.
scenes.narration: In humans, the eminences are seen as the main source too. But cortical progenitors also make some inhibitory neurons.

scenes.tts: Most cortical interneurons start outside the cortex. What they can read helps decide where they go.
scenes.visual: Closing card: born outside the cortex, steered by what the cell can read.
scenes.narration: Most cortical interneurons start outside the cortex. What they can read helps decide where they go.
